variant_policy: Precisely one labeled adaptation per selected authored bank row; no changes to stored source rows. Two source IDs, not four new source questions.

items.stem: A service lift is descending but its downward speed is decreasing. Taking upward as positive, what direction must its net force point?
changes: A-D option texts shortened; key remains A; original option reasons withheld from first attempt; original text retained in source-rows.v1.json

scaffolds.author: NLM-PROD1
scaffolds.text: Name the direction of travel, what happens to speed, and which force quantity is being asked for. Does travel direction alone decide net-force direction?

scaffolds.author: NLM-PROD1
scaffolds.text: Treat a downward velocity as a negative number. Compare an earlier and later velocity when the downward speed is shrinking. Which value is closer to zero, and what does their change per second mean?

scaffolds.author: NLM-PROD1
scaffolds.text: Use the vertical form of Newton's second law, ΣFᵧ = maᵧ. The mass is positive. First infer the acceleration sign from the change in signed velocity, then decide the force direction yourself.

reasoning: The lift moves downward, but its downward speed decreases. Velocity is therefore becoming less negative on an upward-positive axis.
A later velocity minus an earlier velocity is positive, so the acceleration points upward.
By Newton's second law, ΣFᵧ = maᵧ. Because mass is positive, net force is upward.
teacher.check: If the downward speed were constant instead, acceleration and net force would both be zero. Moving down alone does not determine force direction.

feedback.A: This is the intended net-force direction. Compare your written justification with the signed-velocity reasoning below.
feedback.B: This identifies the direction of travel, not necessarily the direction of acceleration. Compare two velocity values.
feedback.C: A steady slowing is still a change in velocity. Zero net force would mean constant velocity.
feedback.D: Mass affects magnitude, but a positive mass does not obscure the direction when acceleration direction is known.

items.stem: Two small robots pull against the ends of the same taut strap. Robot A pulls the strap left with 40 N. Which two forces make a Newton-third-law pair at A's connection to the strap?

options.A: A pulls the strap; gravity pulls A.
options.B: A pulls the strap; B pulls the strap.
options.C: A pulls the strap; the strap pulls A.
options.D: The strap pulls A; the floor pushes A.

changes: Source A (correct) moved to C and rewritten in parallel verb form; source C moved to A; B and D rewritten in parallel verb form; resulting key C; magnitude and direction conditions kept in stem; source remains unchanged

reasoning: At the A–strap contact, A exerts a force on the strap and the strap exerts a force on A.
The paired forces act on different objects, have the same magnitude (40 N), and point in opposite directions.
Two forces on the strap, or two forces on A, are not each other's Newton-third-law interaction pair.

feedback.A: These are different interactions, not two directions of one A–strap contact.
feedback.B: Both of these forces are exerted on the strap. They do not make an action–reaction pair with each other.
feedback.C: These are forces at the same contact, with different objects receiving each force.
feedback.D: Both forces act on A and come from different interactions.

PHYS-NLM-001.reason: One signed-motion inference followed by Newton II; a single decisive mapping to the force sign remains.

PHYS-NLM-002.secondary: EXPLAIN when learner independently supplies a why
PHYS-NLM-002.reason: The option choice classifies an interaction pair using the two participating bodies; it does not require a causal explanation of why a relation holds. Written justification is captured but not machine graded.
